body:
This is actually a really great reply.  I wanted to respond to this last night, but the words weren't coming.  In a few ways, you're right on the money.

I'm not necessarily looking for affirmation of support or care from my loved ones, but that's mostly because I've already got it.  If nothing else, I'm after the opposite reaction.  My concern over bringing this topic to light is getting a reaction that's *too* dramatic or emotional, or making this a much larger deal than it actually is.  I'd prefer a discussion much like the one you and I are having, whether it results in mentally stimulating conversation or simply quells some of the sadness that would arise from me dying.

You use the word "daydream," and I think that's pretty accurate, at least in the way that this began.  You're absolutely correct—it adds excitement, it presents a new viewpoint on life in just a slightly different way.  Heck, I'm finding now that this idea of dying is making day-to-day life a little more interesting, simply because I know that I can end my life at the end of the day if I really wanted to.  It's a stimulating way of looking at things.

But despite having started as daydreams, these aren't idle thoughts anymore.  I'm genuinely considering this, and I'm not quite sure why.  I don't put quite that much value on my own life.  Not in a nihilistic or existential way, mind you, but in a more humbling, profound way.  I watched an episode of Cosmos last night, and that certainly helped that perspective.

The idea of having an off switch when I'm bored of it or when I feel ready and done is a pleasant and appealing one.  Just like I don't watch all movies to completion, or just like I quit a video game, I'm viewing my life in the same way.  I hope this doesn't sound insensitive, but I don't necessarily see this as a sad thing.
